paragraphs: A match air pistol looks nothing like a service weapon. The grip is a moulded orthopaedic block shaped to one shooter's hand, the barrel is surrounded by a compressed air cylinder, and the sights sit on a long adjustable rail. Every element exists to remove variability, which is why the shape is so unusual.
The mesh runs 36,133 polygons and 36,055 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the density in the grip contours, the sight adjusters and the cylinder fittings.

At $49 and built to StemCell specification, it suits shooting sports visualisation and broadcast graphics, Olympic and competition material, sporting goods retail renders, training material and games. On sale since 2026.

Airfield lighting is a coded language written on the ground: colour, spacing and intensity all mean specific things to a pilot, and the fittings themselves are low frangible units designed to break away rather than damage an aircraft that hits one. That frangibility is why they look so slight for equipment that has to survive a runway.
The mesh runs 92,580 polygons and 46,785 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the fitting bodies and the mounting bases.
At $49 it suits airport and airfield visualisation, aviation infrastructure presentation, night approach scenes, simulator projects, training material and games. On sale since 2023.

Adding goggles to a balaclava changes the whole head. The strap compresses the knit across the back of the skull, the frame sits on the fabric rather than on skin, and the eye opening is covered rather than open - which means the figure loses its face entirely and becomes a silhouette. That anonymity is often the point.

The mesh runs 37,312 polygons and 38,019 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 14 texture maps at a wide spread of sizes carrying the knit structure, the strap webbing and the lens tint.

At $49 it suits winter sports advertising, outdoor and tactical clothing visualisation, character set dressing for film, television and games, and retail renders. On sale since 2018, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard head.

This is a deliberate joke with a technical payoff: a balloon animal rendered transparent with a skeleton inside it, borrowing the language of anatomical illustration and applying it to something that has no anatomy at all. The contrast between the glossy inflated shell and the bones within is the whole idea.

The mesh is light at 8,895 polygons and 9,036 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the shell and the internal structure as separate bodies so a transparent material can work over an opaque one.
At $49 it suits art and design presentation, gallery and exhibition visualisation, editorial and conceptual illustration, interior decor renders, advertising and games. On sale since 2022.

A flat-graphic cartoon character in three dimensions is a design problem rather than a modelling one. Characters drawn for animation have shapes that only work from certain angles - a spiked silhouette, a strongly simplified head, features that read as symbols rather than as anatomy - and turning that into a solid object means deciding what the drawing never had to answer.
The mesh is light at 12,438 polygons and 6,573 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits a stylised figure with flat colour surfaces and no fine detail.
At $49 it suits animation and character design reference, merchandise and print visualisation, fan and hobby projects, motion graphics and games. On sale since 2023.

A lifeguard tower is a small building on stilts with a very specific job: raise the observer above the crowd, shade them, and be visible from a distance. That gives it a bright colour, a wide viewing window, a ramp or ladder and a deck rail - and the stilts, which keep it above the tide line.
The mesh is efficient at 27,697 polygons and 29,665 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the frame, the deck and the roof.
At $49 it suits beach and coastal visualisation, tourism and resort marketing, water safety material, film and television set dressing, summer advertising and games. On sale since 2021.

This launcher is a pump action grenade weapon, which is a rare combination: the operator works a slide like a shotgun to chamber the next round from a tube magazine. It was made in tiny numbers, which is exactly why it appears so often in games - it is genuinely unusual and instantly memorable.

The mesh is deliberately minimal at 5,635 polygons and 2,895 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. That budget is a game weapon budget: light enough for a first person view at high frame rates, with the detail carried by texture.

At $49 it suits games and interactive media, film and television armouries, military history visualisation, illustration and print. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a character rig. On sale since 2024.

The trophy is a Victorian claret jug rather than a purpose-designed sports cup, which is why it looks like something from a dining table: a bulbous silver body, a long neck, a scroll handle and a hinged lid with a finial. The engraved names run around the base, and the whole thing is smaller in the hand than photographs suggest.

The mesh is light at 24,104 polygons and 12,298 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the handle, the lid and the base moulding where a polished silver surface needs edges to catch.
At $49 it suits golf and sports broadcast graphics, tournament and ceremony visualisation, sports advertising, memorabilia and print, and games. On sale since 2023.

A folded umbrella is a fabric problem. The canopy wraps around the shaft in a spiral of soft creases, held by a strap, and the ribs make ridges under the cloth. Modelled as a smooth cone it looks like a closed parasol from a stage set rather than something that has been used in weather.
The mesh is efficient at 16,859 polygons and 17,821 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with almost all of the geometry spent on the wrapped folds.

At $49 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits fashion and accessory visualisation, interior and hallway scenes, character set dressing, retail and e-commerce renders, and games. On sale since 2024.

Landing nets vary more than non-anglers expect: rubber mesh for catch and release, knotless nylon for coarse fishing, deep bags for salmon, folding frames for a boat. A scene that shows a tackle shop, a boat or a river bank needs several rather than one, and that variety is what a collection provides.
Supplying them together keeps the handle materials and the mesh treatment consistent, which is what stops a fishing scene assembled from separate sources from looking mismatched.
At $49 it suits fishing and outdoor sports visualisation, tackle retail and catalogue renders, riverside and boat scenes, angling advertising and games. On sale since 2024.

A freefall slide is a near-vertical drop with a trapdoor at the top, and its whole visual identity is that first section: a straight steep chute rising far above the surrounding pools, usually in a bright colour so it reads from across a park. The runout at the bottom is long and shallow for obvious reasons.

The mesh runs 92,088 polygons and 101,517 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the fibreglass finish and the joint lines between sections.
At $49 it suits water park and leisure visualisation, resort and hospitality marketing, attraction design presentation, summer advertising and games. On sale since 2020.

A gloved hand is one of the most used images in healthcare communication, and the glove changes the hand: nitrile stretches tight over the knuckles, wrinkles at the wrist and thumb web, and reflects light in a way skin never does. Modelling the glove as a surface over an accurate hand is what makes that work.
The mesh is minimal at 2,546 polygons and 2,592 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits a subject whose realism comes from the material rather than from geometric density.

Three rigged builds share this page at $69, including versions prepared for Cinema 4D and for Maya. The static model at $49 covers medical and clinical visualisation, healthcare and pharmaceutical advertising, laboratory scenes, training material and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2025.

The guidance section is the front of the missile: the seeker, its radome and the electronics behind it, plus the forward control surfaces. Showing it as a separate assembly is how technical and manufacturing material explains a weapon, because a complete missile hides everything that actually makes it work.

The model is built with subdivision geometry at 22,397 polygons and 22,771 vertices with non-overlapping UVs, which is the right approach for a body made entirely of smooth conical and cylindrical surfaces.
At $49 it suits defence engineering and technical presentation, missile manufacturing and supplier marketing, news and documentary graphics, education material and games. On sale since 2021.

A moulded case with a cut foam insert is a specific and very readable object: the outline of the pistol pressed into the foam, magazine cutouts beside it, and the ribbed shell of the case around them. That silhouette in the foam tells the viewer what is missing when the case is empty, which is why it works so well in imagery.
The mesh runs 48,771 polygons and 49,091 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the foam cutouts, the latches and the case ribbing.

At $49 and built to StemCell specification, it suits firearms retail and catalogue renders, shooting sports material, security and law enforcement visualisation, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2025.
